paper.title: XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models

replaced_predictor: The response judge only: the three-way classification of a model response to an XSTest prompt as full compliance / full refusal / partial refusal (Section 4.2 manual taxonomy; Section 4.5 + Appendix D automated judges: prefix string-match and zero-shot GPT-4). Not the generative safety policy of any model.

source.licence: Prompts CC-BY-4.0 (repo LICENSE). Model completions 'subject to the original licenses specified by Meta, Mistral and OpenAI' (README). Treated as not redistributable here: only IDs + row SHA-256s are frozen; items() rebuilds from data/raw/xstest.
source.fields: model_completions/*.csv: id (v2-1..v2-450), type (18 prompt types; 'contrast_*' = unsafe), prompt, completion, annotation_1, annotation_2, agreement, final_label (1_full_compliance | 2_full_refusal | 3_partial_refusal)

frozen.fields: id (xstest-<model>-<prompt id>), model, row (0-based row in that model's completions CSV), sha256 (gauntlet.tasks.xstest.row_sha256: all CSV columns + model)
frozen.reference: data/frozen/xstest/reference_evaluators.json: GPT-4 and StrMatch judges' agreement with the human final labels and human inter-annotator agreement, derived from the release
frozen.jev_input: state {question: completion-file prompt, response: completion}; prompt type, safety label and model identity are not sent

test_n_resolution: The 450 v2 prompts are 250 safe and 200 unsafe (contrast_*) prompts. The judged unit is a (prompt, completion) pair: 5 models x 450 = 2,250 human-labelled completions, all released; all are used. Human labels reproduce paper Table 2 'Annotation' and Table 5 totals exactly; per-model annotator agreement flags reproduce Section 4.2 (96.4 / 95.8 / 97.6 / 93.8 / 98.4%). Note: Section 4.3 text says '200 safe prompts' but Table 2 header and the release have 250.

english_verification.metadata: Prompts hand-written in English by the authors (Section 3); completions are the models' replies to them.
english_verification.method: langid 1.1.6 (all languages) on every prompt and completion in all 5 files (4,500 fields), plus non-ASCII character ratio > 5%.
english_verification.result: 40 flags = the same 8 prompts x 5 files, all short English questions misidentified (e.g. v2-38 -> tl, v2-399 -> nl, v2-377 -> fr). No completion flagged. No rows dropped.

data_checks.prompt_text_differences: v2-195 only: the completion files (and both auto-eval files) hold the prompt wording the models answered; xstest_prompts.csv at this commit words this prompt slightly differently. Jev gets the completion-file text.
data_checks.gpt4_evaluator_non_label_outputs: 11 MistrI rows (GPT-4 refused to classify); counted as full compliance as in paper footnote 10
data_checks.table2_reproduced: All 30 cells (manual / StrMatch / GPT-4 x 5 models x safe/unsafe, full and partial) recomputed from the release equal the printed Table 2; asserted by the prepare script.

metric.primary: accuracy: three-way agreement of Jev's label with the human final_label over 2,250 completions
metric.secondary: macro-F1 and per-class F1 over the three classes; Cohen's kappa; binary refusal view (full+partial refusal vs compliance) accuracy / macro-F1 / F1(refusal); Table 2 replica (refusal rates per model x safe/unsafe) with mean absolute error vs human rates and Spearman correlation of models' total refusal rates with human rates

reference_evaluators.provenance: Our computation from the released automated_evaluation_labels vs final_label; the paper prints only Table 2 refusal rates, which these label files reproduce exactly.

deviations: The paper reports no agreement/accuracy/F1 for its automated judges, only refusal rates (Table 2) and a qualitative ranking claim. Reference numbers are derived by us from the released per-response judge labels (which reproduce Table 2 exactly).

Jev receives the paper's GPT-4 judge prompt (Appendix D) verbatim as instruction + criteria, with the QUESTION/RESPONSE slots moved into the state. The paper's manual annotators also had per-prompt-type guidance (Appendix C, Tables 3-4); like the GPT-4 judge, Jev does not.

The paper collected completions with system prompts for some models (Section 4.1); the released completion files do not include system prompts and the GPT-4 judge was not shown them, so neither is Jev.
